learning_objective: 🎯 Move beyond coin flips! Calculate the chances of complex, interconnected events and update your predictions when new information arrives.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: This calculates the probability of event A happening, GIVEN that event B has already happened. Knowing B occurred shrinks your sample space. We write this as $P(A|B)$.
Two events are independent if the occurrence of one does absolutely nothing to affect the other (like rolling a die and flipping a coin). If independent, $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$.
The ultimate 'Reverse' probability. If you know the final outcome (like picking a defective bulb), Bayes' theorem helps you work backward to find out which factory machine most likely produced it.
A Random Variable assigns a real number to every outcome of an experiment. The probability distribution is simply a neat table showing all possible numbers and their exact chances of happening.

fun_activity.title: 🃏 The Monty Hall Door Problem
fun_activity.instructions: Look up the 'Monty Hall Problem' online. It's a famous puzzle about game shows and doors that perfectly demonstrates Conditional Probability. Try it with a friend using playing cards!

exam_tips: 📌 For Bayes' Theorem questions, always clearly define your events $E_1, E_2, E_3$ (the paths) and $A$ (the known outcome). Formulating the equation is 80% of the battle.
📌 Read carefully: 'Mutually Exclusive' means $P(A \cap B) = 0$ (they can't happen together). 'Independent' means $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$. Do not mix them up!
📌 To verify a Probability Distribution table, add up all the probabilities in the bottom row. They MUST sum to exactly 1.
quick_recap: ⭐ Conditional probability updates the odds based on new clues.
⭐ Independent events don't affect each other; multiply their probabilities.
⭐ Bayes' theorem works backward from results to causes.
